ITT: depressingly few actual Pagans. Well... rolls up sleeves

Edit: Voat messed up and posted four times, sorry! I deleted three of them.

Childhood in the Church

I was raised Lutheran in my early years. I'm mid-30s now, so this happened mostly in the 80s and early 90s. Lutherans are hit-and-miss, I've found; half of them focus on "God loves you and God loves me, therefore vicariously I love you and that's awesome" aspect while the other half have pastors who will sermonize in the middle of a wedding about how (paraphrasing) "this is a real wedding and gay weddings aren't." Anyway, I was part of the former type of congregation and it helped form a solid understanding of morality and how rituals work in a group setting, but as my parents were lazy about indoctrination I never really felt the "spark" that is Faith. I pretty much just went through the motions.

My parents got divorced after I finished 6th grade. My sister fell back on the rock of her Faith for emotional support. I fell back on the excessively rational part of my mind. I was that weird emotionless kid who worshiped at the altar of Science. You know how it is. My Dad's family was the side that cared about church; my mom didn't make me go anymore.

In High School, my Dad's side started asking why they'd never been to a Confirmation for me (basically sunday school graduation). So I gave the church another chance. I went, I studied the Bible, I got pushed around by the same asshole kids that I dealt with at school, and I thought hard about what was being taught. Two things stuck with me:

"You should be here for yourself, not because other people want you to"

Damn. And then:

"Confirmation is the act of dedicating your life to the service of God."

Well, shit. I thought HARD about it and I felt like I had no strong feelings about God's existence. So I dropped out and never went back. Well, I went back once for some youth ministry grad my sister had or something, and there was a hella awkward conversation with the one really nice overenthusiastic teacher who said she missed me and I was all "yeah, I don't... no."

TL;DR: Raised Christian, felt no spark.

Middle year Agnosticism

Agnosticism is the true faith of the lazy and the excessively rational. Either Apathetic ("It doesn't matter if there's a God or not") or Aggressive ("You can't prove that's a real God or even the right God so I'm hedging my bets and staying neutral"), folks like me who leave the Church because of a failure to believe usually spend time agnostic. I respected the Church and the good things it did for individuals and communities, and I was happy for folks like my sister who could Believe with all her heart and find strength there, but I stood apart from it.

The trouble is, I'm a person who deals poorly with stress. It comes from the bullying I've hinted at and the broken family and blah blah blah basically I've been pushed so far past my limits for so long at a stretch that I can't vent stress and tend to slowly build toward a mental breakdown over and over.

The fourth semester of University was when my breakdown started to happen. Even with no responsibilities but my classes and my IRC anime community (fuck you I was a nerd and it was 2000-2002), I felt myself cracking under the pressure. Finally, I decided I needed a change. This was around when Buffy was in its 4th-5th season when they (REALLY poorly) shoehorned Wicca into the show, so I ordered some Scott Cunningham books off Amazon and started reading them to see if it spoke to me.

TL;DR:

“No man is an island, entire of itself.” ― John Donne

Getting my Feet Wet

Scott Cunningham's books are wonderful and if you want to "get" Pagans then I suggest giving this a read. He describes some critical concepts like the idea that Religion is a mask we place upon the power that created the Universe and the fact that one's Religion is a very personal thing, that it is good to practice with like-minded groups but that ultimately it's only within yourself that Faith can happen and you should never let someone else dictate your Faith to you. He also taught me to find beauty in the universe's very existence and a bunch of other hippy-dippy shit I'm sure OP isn't too interested in.

I was Wiccan and then "Eclectic Pagan" for a long time after that. I took great comfort in praying to a pair of faceless Male and Female Gods (Protip: if someone prays only to "The Goddess" then she is a bad Wiccan... Wicca is about balance). The Rede gave me a moral compass again in a time when my thoughts had been getting darker and darker in a scary way. Lik, intense visions of violence scary. And through a local Yahoo group I made like-minded friends who got me out of my basement place and socializing again, since I had withdrawn from my toxic University friends.

It was a pretty good time to be me, although the Pagan community, being young (Wicca went mainstream in the 1950s and before then Pagans were few and far between), is prone to a lot of infighting and dramawhoring. Eventually the group that I was part of sort of scattered all at once, and I was alone again, but my beliefs kept me fairly mentally healthy.

TL;DR: becoming a witch helped heal my mind.

Finding my True Path

Eventually, my lazy Paganism wasn't enough for me. I needed more. I'd been participating on Pagan Forum for long enough that I felt like I was teaching far more than I was learning, but I still had never felt the fervent Faith of the True Believer. So I started researching some other deities. My wife had just had me read a really fascinating realistic-type fiction series about Arthur's knights, wherein characters would worship Gods from wildly different cultures in a sort of "patchwork pantheon" and with that as my goal, I started researching Deities that might represent aspects of my world.

Imagine there's a literal path, and there's this kid on the path. Your godchild. And this kid walks down the path for years, two steps in front of you, making choices at crossroads. And you stand behind, whispering in his ear or nudging him left or right, keeping him from falling off the path or getting killed by something but largely letting him make mistakes and learn for himself. And then one day, he stops in his tracks. He thinks, he reads a book, and then he looks around. He looks left, looks right, then finally looks behind him and says "Godmother?"

You kiss him, and then slap him for ignoring you for so long.

That's what Sekhmet did to me.

After all those years of wandering around not even knowing that a part of my heart was missing, suddenly I felt what I could only describe as a fire in my chest. Even now I'm excited to talk about it. I felt Faith. I felt the unshakable knowledge that this is my truth. That all my life, one particular "Mask of Deity" had been looking out for me, had believed in me, and wanted me in Her service. I was pretty much overjoyed. I gave some other Gods a fair shake, just to be sure, but Hephaestus and Nyx were silent. Sekhmet was not. I felt what I felt, and I only felt it for one entity.

I read all I could find about Sekhmet, about Kemetic Reconstruction, and I formed a system of morals based on this new knowledge, the idea that the Goddess looking after me was one of dual nature: Wrath and War, and Love and Healing. I ditched my "play it safe" attitude and decided that my role was to turn the other cheek in order to put more power into my backhand; to identify the problem in any situation and attack it until it was not a problem anymore. To watch over my family, as I now have a wife and son, by destroying anything that threatens them (usually debt or mental health issues, but these battles can be metaphorical).

My wife found a similar fire in a Norse deity, and we have a sort of truce in the house between them. Our son has been given the agency to find his own path when he's ready.

TL;DR: Sekhmet is my co-pilot. Always has been, I just never looked on the crew manifest. When you feel Faith, you feel Faith... and when your moral and belief structure fixes the problems in your life, you don't argue with that.
